newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs worried by gene-modified micro-organisms.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs worried by gene-modified micro-organisms.

text.p: Euro-MPs are due on March 12 to approve a controversial proposal to update safety rules imposed on laboratories which want to experiment with changing the genetic make-up of dangerous micro-organisms like the use dangerous viruses like AIDS or Ebola viruses.

The European Parliament is expected to heed its environment committee and demand amendments to tighten up the safety aspects of the draft directive, COM(95)640, which is designed to update a 1990 directive on GMMs to take account of progress in the field of biotechnology.

But Green Euro-MPs and the Christian Democrat author of the parliament's draft report on GMMs are expected to warn that even with the environment committee's amendments the new directive may be too lenient to protect humans and the environment from further health and safety crises like madcow disease.
"No one knows what the dangers of GMMs are," Green group administrator Steve Ammot told Reuters on Wednesday.

Ammot said the Greens felt GMMs were not being controlled properly and that until researchers had more practical experience in this new and promising field the European Union should err on the side of safety.

When parliament's environment committee adopted Antonios Trakatellis's draft report on GMMs, it agreed GMMs should be classified more clearly according to the degree of health risk they pose, so that industry and the authorities will know exactly what precautions they have to take to prevent accidents.

The committee also agreed with the Greek Christian Democrat's demand for laboratories conducting GMM experiments to be so insulated as to prevent GMMs coming into contact with the general population and the surrounding environment.
The European Commission has proposed that contained environments should limit but not necessarily prevent contact between GMMs and the outside world.
But the environment committee did not accept Trakatellis's proposals for stricter authorisation procedures for labs wanting to experiment with GMMs.

Parliament's two largest groups, the Socialists and the Christian Democrats, thought the rapporteur's proposals imposed too much red tape on researchers at a time when Europe's biotechnology industry was struggling to compete with its American rival, an aide to Trakatellis told Reuters.

David Bowe, a leading British Socialist member of the environment committee, said the committee agreed that laboratories should not be able to use highly infectious viruses like AIDS or Ebola without formal approval from the authorities.
But they thought laboratories experimenting with relatively safe micro-organisms should only have to notify the authorities before starting their experiments.

As a counterweight to this greater flexibility, the committee would insist on laboratories taking out sufficient liability insurance to compensate all people likely to be harmed if their containment and control measures failed, Bowe said.
"People who experiment with these things must be responsible for their actions," he said.
This is a view shared by the Greens, who say they will vote against the draft report next week if the civil liability clause is not included.

Like Trakatellis, himself a professor in biotechnology, the Greens are worried the proposed authorisation procedures are too lax and plan to table amendments requiring laboratories to seek the active consent of the authorities before using micro-organisms in GMM work, even those in the lower-risk classes, such as salmonella and tetanus.
